title: Kenneth Rogoff - Podcast - In Good Company - Norges Bank Investment Management

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Kenneth Rogoff - Podcast - In Good Company - Norges Bank Investment Management.docx

speakers: Kenneth Rogoff (Harvard economist, former IMF chief economist, author)
Nicolai Tangen (CEO, Norges Bank Investment Management; interviewer)
summary: Podcast with Kenneth Rogoff on tariffs, the dollar, China, inflation, central bank independence and sovereign debt. He sees a 1970s/Nixon-style political economy: tariffs, a coming inflation burst, price controls and financial repression, higher rates, and a gradually declining dollar footprint.

coverage.note: US policy chaos, Nixon analogy, tariffs forecast
tariffs and inflation, Europe response, recession risk, sentiment split
partisan sentiment, subsidies, no Trump put
dollar footprint peak, reserve currency change, de-dollarization
sanctions, China GDP doubt, commodity exporters, deflation
China japanification, manufacturing shift, India, inflation remission
academic inflation blind spot, independence, next inflation burst, debt
cyber war, debt to rates or inflation, Fed independence, climate
price controls, financial repression, Fed vs politics, sentiment
Fed mission, forward guidance, supply chain inflation
central bank mistake, US debt, secular stagnation critique, deficit
debt sudden stops, defense spending, default unlikely, real yields
interest costs, dollar weakness, Reinhart-Rogoff validation, debt and growth
debt and rates, AI deflation, AI speed, GDP
AI inflation, tech-bubble crises, crypto, contrarian views

completeness_estimate: 0.90 - first reader captured nearly all of the macro arguments (tariffs, dollar, China, inflation outlook, central bank independence, debt); missed some political-economy supports (tariff popularity, bipartisan protectionism), sequencing remarks, the default and bank-regulation points, and a few host-quoted theses.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it feels a little like the 70s to me. Trump actually feels a little like Nixon to me
claims.claim: The current policy regime (tariffs, fracturing globalization, pressure on institutions) is analogous to the 1970s Nixon era, which implies a wild macro ride and an inflation-prone backdrop.
claims.conditions: Historical analogy, not a rule

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: we undermine the institutions that are the bedrock of US exceptionalism
claims.claim: Undermining rule of law and the credibility of US commitments (e.g. paying debts) erodes the foundation of US exceptionalism and the premium assets in the US enjoy.
claims.conditions: If institutional credibility is actually damaged

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: maybe we'll have more manufacturing jobs, maybe, but things will cost a lot more
claims.claim: Reshoring via protectionism may add some manufacturing jobs but raises costs and lowers incomes versus an integrated global economy.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the uh on the order of uh uh I don't know at least 10 you know 15% 20%
claims.claim: A year ahead the US will still have tariffs on Europe of roughly 10-20%, with European retaliation and a lot of noise.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: if we just slapped on 20% tariffs, it would be very bad, like a big tax hike
claims.claim: Broad 20% tariffs act like a large tax increase, reduce trade and disrupt supply chains.
claims.conditions: Not the end of the world if combined with deregulation and pro-innovation measures
claims.testable: partly: tariff shocks can be studied (2018 episode)

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: It would not be the end of the world if together with that Trump did a bunch of sensible things deregulation
claims.claim: The net effect of tariffs depends on whether they are paired with offsetting supply-side reforms such as deregulation.
claims.conditions: Offset only if deregulation and innovation policy accompany tariffs

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the real problem is the randomness and what it signals about other things to come such as central bank independence
claims.claim: The unpredictability of tariff policy is the main damage because it signals further institutional shocks such as threats to central bank independence.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the the problem is more uh innovation slowing growth over the longer run
claims.claim: Tariffs give a short-term price level hit (higher prices, lower quality) but the bigger cost is slower innovation and lower long-run growth, not lasting inflation.
claims.direction: inflation up short term, growth down long term

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: of course we pay the tariffs dollar for Every study shows that
claims.claim: US consumers bear tariffs dollar for dollar through higher prices, as studies of the 2018 tariffs show.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: military often provides the funding early on for uh tech uh tech startups, tech investment
claims.claim: European tech independence and defence build-up are linked because military spending funds early-stage tech, per the Draghi report logic.

correction.issue: Conflates two points. Rogoff says the Draghi report made the point that Europe has lagged in tech and should be more independent; the link that military spending often funds early-stage tech is Rogoff's own comment, not the Draghi report's.
correction.fix: Rogoff: Draghi's report argued Europe has lagged in tech and needs more tech independence; he adds that defence and tech are connected because military spending often supplies early funding for tech start-ups.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it kind of forces Europe to g be more assertive, to be more independent in a way that I think has been a long time coming
claims.claim: US trade pressure is a forcing event pushing Europe toward greater strategic and economic independence.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the nature of the recession we might get is a loss of confidence
claims.claim: US recession odds rose sharply and the mechanism would be a confidence shock among consumers rather than an oil shock, pandemic or financial crisis.
claims.conditions: If consumer sentiment collapses broadly

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: The indicators for the Democratic voters are just off the charts terrible
claims.claim: Consumer sentiment splits sharply by political affiliation: Democrats are extremely pessimistic (and expect inflation to soar) while Republicans are upbeat.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it can cause a recession because yeah you the the Republicans are not going to spend enough to make up for what the Democrats aren't spending
claims.claim: Partisan divergence in sentiment can depress aggregate spending because the optimistic group does not offset the spending cut by the pessimistic group.
claims.conditions: When pessimism is large and one-sided
claims.testable: partly: could test spending by party-lean

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's better to have an environment where the regulation and the general uh work environment for companies is good and makes them want to invest
claims.claim: Tariffs and subsidies are both weak ways to attract investment; a good regulatory and business environment works better and subsidy wars are effectively trade war.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: So, I don't I don't believe in a Trump put put.
claims.claim: Do not rely on a presidential put: the president is convinced tariffs are good, so markets should not assume a quick policy reversal after drawdowns.
claims.conditions: If the president has conviction rather than just bluffing
claims.testable: partly: reaction to market drops testable but sample small

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: we sort of reached the peak 10 years ago in terms of the dollar's footprint and dominance in the global economy
claims.claim: The dollar's global footprint (reserves, transactions, invoicing) peaked around 2015 and is slowly declining.
claims.indicator: dollar share of reserves, transactions, invoicing
claims.testable: yes: reserve share and invoicing data

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it is a surprise that the euro right now is a regional currency
claims.claim: Challengers have fallen short: the euro is only regional, the yen barely used and the renminbi less, so the dollar keeps top position despite its decline.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the global currency normally changes slowly
claims.claim: Reserve-currency transitions are slow, taking about a century (Spanish peso example), so the dollar fades gradually and a sudden loss of status is unlikely.
claims.conditions: Slow death, challenger rises over time

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: they want to expand its footprint. more things priced in Chinese currency
claims.claim: China is expanding renminbi pricing and lending and building its own clearing rails to reduce exposure to US sanction power.
claims.indicator: renminbi share of trade settlement and loans

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: If it touches the dollar, most of it goes to the United States.
claims.claim: Dollar clearing and messaging control give the US visibility and sanction leverage, which motivates China (after Russia sanctions) to build alternative clearing mechanisms.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: if your prices are going down continually and you're telling me you have 5% growth, I don't believe you
claims.claim: China's official 5% GDP growth is not credible alongside persistent deflation; true growth is probably around 2-3%, and the figures are manufactured.
claims.testable: partly: can cross-check with alternative indicators

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's very big on uh energy exporters and commodity exporters
claims.claim: A China slowdown hits energy and commodity exporters (Norway, US as energy producer, Brazil, Argentina); a growth rebound to 8% would help them.
claims.testable: yes: commodity demand vs China growth

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: that that loss of confidence has pushed interest rates down
claims.claim: Chinese households lost confidence, consumption collapsed and rates fell into deflation, unlike rising rates elsewhere.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: If they push that money out to the rest of the world in the form of trade surpluses and such, it'll have a big effect
claims.claim: China's excess savings could be exported through trade surpluses, but the rest of the world is unlikely to accept that.
claims.conditions: Depends on trading partners' tolerance (tariffs)

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the slow growth the housing problem the overbuilding in infrastructure and housing the similarities are are really quite remarkable
claims.claim: China is in a Japan-style balance-sheet crisis (deflation, slow growth, overbuilt housing), lasting longer than Sweden's quick recovery and likely a few more years.
claims.conditions: Over-centralization of power worsens long-term growth

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: So they need to go back to this growth model where the private sector leads and the states not doing everything.
claims.claim: Crushing the private sector (Jack Ma, party members on boards) harms Chinese growth and makes Chinese tech hard to invest in despite its quality.
claims.direction: China tech equity risk premium up
claims.conditions: If the state keeps reasserting control

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's been great for Japan, for Korea, for Singapore, Malaysia, even Indonesia and India
claims.claim: Manufacturing and new investment diversifying away from China (China plus one) benefits Japan, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and India.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: The big thing is that housing, real estate's plummeting
claims.claim: The main driver of China's slow growth is the property collapse and panicked consumers who distrust the government, not the manufacturing shift.
claims.testable: yes: property price and sales data

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: optimistic but it's hard to get euphoric about India because it's just so hard to govern a country of 1.4 billion people
claims.claim: India grows faster than China with new infrastructure but monopoly concentration, tariffs and governance difficulty cap enthusiasm.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: So I have always thought inflation was in remission and not dead.
claims.claim: Inflation was in remission, not dead, after the 2000s-2010s low-inflation era; academic work that assumed no inflation was wrong.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: hardwired into all the top journal papers that have been coming out
claims.claim: Academic macro models hard-wire the no-inflation assumption inherited from central-bank messaging, which biases research and consensus views.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: they were also lucky because globalization helped the rise of China helped
claims.claim: The low-inflation era resulted partly from tailwinds (globalization, China's rise, anti-populist consensus, hands-off politics) not just central bank skill; those tailwinds have faded.
claims.conditions: Tailwinds reverse when globalization fractures and independence erodes

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: inflation's a political economy problem. And if you don't really have central bank independence
claims.claim: Inflation is a political economy problem; without real central bank independence a country periodically runs into inflation trouble.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: there's going to be another big burst of inflation similar to what we saw in the uh after the pandemic
claims.claim: Another large inflation burst similar to post-pandemic is expected within about 5-7 years (possibly sooner), triggered by a shock that corners central banks.
claims.conditions: Needs an unforeseen shock

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the pressures are going to be towards worrying about having a recession and they're just not going to be able to stand up to the politics
claims.claim: In the next shock central banks will prioritize avoiding recession over fighting inflation because political pressure is stronger than in 2008-2009.
claims.conditions: Depends on the nature of the shock; a 2008-type shock would not do it

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: my best guess is that both parties want it to go up and it will it it's going to put upward pressure on interest rates
claims.claim: Rising US debt that both parties want to expand will put upward pressure on interest rates, and raising rates to fight inflation is hard when rates are already high.
claims.testable: partly: debt supply and term premium studies

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: We can say what happens once the shock hits.
claims.claim: Inflation shocks cannot be timed any better than financial crises: one can describe the response after the shock but not forecast the date.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it cuts growth and then the government uh does stuff to try to hold up consumption by spending money
claims.claim: A shock like a cyber war or pandemic cuts growth, then fiscal support to hold up consumption drives inflation.
claims.conditions: Shock must be large and met by fiscal expansion

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: debt doesn't just mechanically turn into inflation. That's wrong. It either turns into higher interest rates or inflation.
claims.claim: Government debt does not mechanically become inflation; it ends in either higher interest rates or inflation, depending on central bank behavior.
claims.conditions: Which one depends on whether the central bank is independent or packed with doves

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: pack the central bank with people who we call doves
claims.claim: Political appointment of dovish central bankers is a path from debt to inflation.
claims.conditions: If appointments tilt dovish

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: there's a lot of pressures on on the Fed's independence coming from both sides of the spectrum
claims.claim: The Fed lacks constitutional protection like the ECB, and pressure on its independence comes from both left and right, so independence could disappear quickly.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: natural catastrophes which lower output and put upward pressure
claims.claim: Worsening storms and climate extremes are arriving sooner and reduce output while raising prices.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: you then have a choice do you raise interest rates or do you allow inflation to go up and I bet we'd allow inflation to go up
claims.claim: In a climate shock met by large spending, policymakers would likely tolerate inflation rather than raise rates.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: Fed independence is a new thing. Uh central bank independence is a new thing.
claims.claim: Central bank independence is an experiment only about 40 years old; historically banks sat inside treasuries, so it is politically reversible.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: that's why inflation's down because you have central bank independence
claims.claim: Opponents argue independence is no longer needed because inflation is low, but inflation is low because of independence.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: We are going to start to get inflation pressures.
claims.claim: After DOGE cuts, big tax cuts and stimulus (with a recession as political cover), inflation pressures will emerge and the president will dislike them.
claims.conditions: After fiscal stimulus phase

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: I think we're going to see Nixon like price controls like we saw in the 1970s.
claims.claim: Expect Nixon-style price controls and other controls in response to inflation, rather than waiting for the fourth year of the term.
claims.conditions: If inflation rises while politics blocks rate hikes

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: financial repression which we have to some degree now since the financial crisis where banks and financial firms are forced to hold more debt at ending up at lower returns than they'd like
claims.claim: Financial repression (forcing banks and financial firms to hold government debt at low returns) is already partially in place and likely to expand.
claims.direction: govt bond demand up, yields suppressed

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: It works for a little while and then eventually, you know, things spin out of control.
claims.claim: Price controls and financial repression work only temporarily before inflation spins out of control.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: if left to its own devices, it will raise interest rates
claims.claim: The Fed, if left independent, would raise rates if inflation rose even with strong jobs, setting up a showdown with politicians.
claims.conditions: Absent pressure from Congress or the president

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: consumer sentiment 70% of consumers are 70% of consumption
claims.claim: Consumer sentiment matters more than business sentiment because consumption is about 70% of the economy, though the Fed gives professional business forecasts extra weight.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: pushing the Fed to be the leader in climate change is just a ticket to having it lose its focus
claims.claim: The Fed should keep to inflation; academic economists leaning toward climate, inequality and social justice are naive, and Congress should handle those goals.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: markets don't believe it. And then you get to a year later and the Fed's a little bit tied its hands by giving this forward guidance
claims.claim: Dot plots and extended forward guidance are overdone: markets discount them and later they constrain the central bank.
claims.testable: partly: dot plot vs realized path

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the main reason everyone was slow to increase rates really was that they wanted to be
claims.claim: Central banks were slow to hike in 2021-22 because conditions looked like they could get really bad and they wanted to be cautious.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: Why didn't the price of paper towels come down? Why didn't the price of everything come down? That was a central bank mistake.
claims.claim: The supply-chain explanation fails because prices did not fall when supply chains normalized, so the 2021-22 inflation was a central bank mistake.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: should have raised interest rates sooner
claims.claim: Central banks should have raised rates sooner rather than look through a big shock as temporary.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: on its current path, it's going to have to get resolved by inflation
claims.claim: US debt on its current path will ultimately be resolved partly through inflation.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: They're looking at the recent past too much. And if you look at a longer time period, you would see that this period of low interest rates was going to go away.
claims.claim: Secular stagnation and permanent low-rate views suffered recency bias; longer history showed the low-rate era would end.
claims.testable: yes: long samples of real rates

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: big inflation that's going to partly bring the debt down but this time interest rates are going to go up a lot more
claims.claim: The next inflation burst will lift rates far more than last time because investors forgave central banks once but will not again.
claims.conditions: Following a shock that triggers inflation

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: The Congressional Budget Office, I think, has it going to 65 trillion in 10 years.
claims.claim: US runs a deficit of about 7% of GDP and debt of 36 trillion could reach 65 trillion in 10 years per CBO, so adjustments (higher taxes or lower spending) will be needed.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: So, they've both been telling this fiction, which I think now interest rates are saying the markets don't believe.
claims.claim: Both the left (debt is free) and right (tax cuts pay for themselves) hold fictions that markets no longer believe, visible in higher rates.
claims.testable: partly: growth effects of tax cuts measurable

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: when you go to an emerging market uh that borrows in dollars, it can happen very suddenly
claims.claim: Debt crises hit suddenly for countries borrowing in foreign currency (Greece, EM), unlike the US.
claims.conditions: Foreign-currency borrowers

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: because we we have the inflation card to play and you can play it a little, you can play it a lot
claims.claim: The US can inflate away debt, so a sudden sharp rise in coupon demanded is unlikely; the effect will show up gradually in interest rates.
claims.conditions: Issuer of own major currency

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: having really high debt for an advanced country weighs on growth because it reduces your options
claims.claim: High debt in advanced countries weighs on growth by limiting stimulus and investment options.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's not just going to 2%. There's decades of underinvestment that need to be made up for.
claims.claim: Europe must raise defense spending well above 2% of GDP because the US cannot project power in two or three regions at once (US defense is 3.5% of GDP vs 8% at end of Cold War).

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: They have a lot of financial repression in Japan.
claims.claim: Large-currency issuers avoid default by using financial repression and rules, as Japan does with very high debt and low growth.
claims.conditions: Issuer of a major currency

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: the 10-year inflation index Treasury when Larry Summers did a secular stagnation speech was average zero over those 10 years. That got to minus one. Now it's around two.
claims.claim: The 10-year real (TIPS) yield swung from about -1 to +2, a 3-point change, ending the secular-stagnation low-rate regime.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: a trillion. And that's very painful.
claims.claim: US interest payments rose from about 250 billion to nearly 1 trillion, which is painful though adjustable for now.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: a lot of the big problems are inside the unwillingness to confront debt, concerns about the independence of the central bank
claims.claim: Internal problems (unconfronted debt, central bank independence) will weaken the dollar and its footprint, as with Rome.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: how much housing prices fell. It was remarkably uh on our on our averages.
claims.claim: Post-financial-crisis outcomes (unemployment rise and duration, stock and housing declines) matched historical averages in Reinhart-Rogoff, so historical averages are good priors.
claims.indicator: unemployment, stocks, house prices after crises

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: look at the low debt countries and how much they were able to stimulate their economies, they did better.
claims.claim: After the GFC low-debt countries stimulated more and did better; Germany is using fiscal space saved for a rainy day; Italy, Japan, France growth held back by debt.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: Running deficits is great. It's good for your economy. Having a big debt is not good for your economy because it prevents you from as easily running deficits.
claims.claim: Deficits help in downturns, but a large accumulated debt limits the ability to run them when needed.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: tell me what interest rate you're paying and I can give you a lot better answer
claims.claim: Debt sustainability depends on the interest rate; the debate assuming zero rates forever was wrong and rate changes now make adjustment more painful but not immediately forcing.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: interest rates were negative, so wasn't very hard to persuade the Germans to do it
claims.claim: With positive interest rates, the next European crisis package will be harder to agree on than the negative-rate pandemic one.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's possible that technology will produce an effect like globalization did putting downward pressure on wages and putting downward uh pressure on prices
claims.claim: AI may exert disinflationary pressure like globalization did, though also bring worker displacement and political tension.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: What worries me is that it's going to be so fast. Humans, mankind, will not be able to adjust to it.
claims.claim: The risk of AI is the speed of change, which could cause chaotic adjustment in workplaces and warfare.

claims.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
claims.quote: Last year probably 15% I suspect this year we'll see 20% efficiency gain.
claims.claim: NBIM saw about 15% efficiency gain from AI-assisted coding last year and expects 20% this year.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: it's been a long time since GDP was a really accurate measure of the economy
claims.claim: GDP has long been a poor measure of the economy because it misses many things, and AI-driven labor change adds uncertainty about jobs.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: I don't buy this idea that don't worry about inflation because this is going to make everything cheaper.
claims.claim: Do not ignore inflation because of AI: political pressure on central banks is strong, so inflation will be a problem for decades even as AI transforms life.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: a lot of financial crises have come because there's a new technology and everybody gets all excited about it
claims.claim: New technologies (steam, railroads, airplanes) cause hard-to-value excitement and sudden valuation collapses, so AI valuations carry crisis potential.
claims.conditions: New technology with unclear value

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: look for it coming out of crypto rather than necessarily high valuations of AI firms
claims.claim: If a financial crisis comes it is more likely to emerge from crypto than AI valuations because regulation makes the regulated system more robust.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: I was sort of all alone in arguing that real interest rates weren't going to be low forever
claims.claim: Rogoff's contrarian calls: real rates not low forever, China not growing to the moon, dollar's peak passed; he claims these are less fringe now.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: And Trump says, and I hope he has a plan, that it's all going to be better on the other side of this, but uh obviously the stock markets are getting nervous.
claims.claim: American exceptionalism has been dented because the hegemon is disrupting its own system, and equity markets are nervous because there may be no plan behind the promise that things will be better after the disruption.
claims.indicator: US equity market sentiment, US policy uncertainty
claims.direction: US equities weaker on policy uncertainty
claims.conditions: April 2025 tariff shock
claims.testable: partly - equity returns versus policy uncertainty index

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: he knows politics better than I do, and he thinks 80% of Americans love terrorists
claims.claim: Tariffs are politically popular with the American public (the caption's 'terrorists' is 'tariffs'; even his well-educated mother liked them), so economists' objections have little political traction and tariffs are less likely to be dropped.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: there's not a lot of open water between really the left where the left was in the US and Trump
claims.claim: Protectionism is bipartisan in the US (Bernie Sanders ran on similar trade positions in 2016), so tariffs are not a one-person quirk and are more likely to persist after the current administration.
claims.indicator: US trade policy stance across parties

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: You don't have one election in France or Germany suddenly changing everything. Change a lot but not everything.
claims.claim: Europe's institutional stability (single elections change a lot but not everything) makes it a more stable geopolitical counterweight to a US whose direction can reverse with each presidential election.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: we saw it under Biden where the Republicans thought inflation was way higher than it was and the Democrats thought inflation was way lower than it was
claims.claim: Partisan bias in perceived inflation is symmetric: under Biden Republicans overstated inflation and Democrats understated it, so survey-based sentiment and inflation expectations are contaminated by party identity.
claims.indicator: survey inflation expectations by party (University of Michigan type surveys)
claims.conditions: polarised electorates
claims.testable: yes - survey expectations split by party

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: China is certainly thinking about uh, you know, provoking the eye of the United States at some point by trying to take over Taiwan and looking at the sanctions
claims.claim: China is weighing a move on Taiwan and has studied the sanctions imposed on Russia, which is why it wants renminbi pricing and its own clearing rails as protection against US financial sanctions.
claims.indicator: renminbi share of trade settlement, CIPS vs SWIFT usage
claims.conditions: Taiwan risk and sanctions exposure
claims.testable: partly - share of renminbi in settlements

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: I'm making a political economy call I'm not saying there's some, you know, constellation of shocks that's just going to happen in a certain way and create inflation
claims.claim: His inflation forecast is a regime-level political-economy call (central banks will not stand firm when a shock arrives), not a point forecast of a specific shock sequence; he does not claim to know the trigger or the date.
claims.direction: higher inflation in the next shock
claims.conditions: politically weakened central banks

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: I think we're going to see him reach into the toolkit. And you know, Fed independence comes later.
claims.claim: Sequence of political responses to inflation: first the executive reaches for tools such as price controls and financial repression, and only later does a direct fight over Fed independence arrive.
claims.indicator: price controls, financial repression measures, Fed independence
claims.conditions: inflation returning under a president averse to higher rates

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: there are people who lose by having interest rates high
claims.claim: Even with strong jobs, high interest rates have losers (young people buying houses and cars), which creates political pressure on the Fed and makes a showdown likely when it hikes against inflation.
claims.indicator: mortgage rates, auto loan rates, political pressure on Fed
claims.conditions: Fed tightening into strong employment

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: If you want to give people more stuff and bigger transfers, all for it, more power to you, but raise taxes.
claims.claim: Concern about debt is not the same as support for austerity: bigger transfers are fine if financed by taxes, but treating deficit spending as a free lunch is the error.

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: It would be so stupid because we we can print money. We don't need to default on our Treasury bonds.
claims.claim: A US default or forced restructuring of Treasuries is not a realistic scenario because the US issues its own currency and can inflate or repress instead, so the risk is inflation or higher yields, not default.
claims.conditions: sovereign issuing its own major currency

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: we put in all these restrictions to make the bank safer that had them basically hold more Fed debt, which is basically Treasury bonds and more
claims.claim: Post-crisis bank safety rules already forced banks to hold more Treasuries, a form of financial repression that creates captive demand for government debt and can be extended further.
claims.indicator: bank holdings of Treasuries, liquidity coverage rules
claims.conditions: regulatory requirements
claims.testable: yes - bank Treasury holdings versus regulatory changes

claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
claims.quote: central bank independence up to this point has worked. It's given people more confidence. It allowed uh debt levels to be higher maybe than they would have otherwise.
claims.claim: Central bank independence has supported confidence and allowed governments to run higher debt levels than otherwise, so any loss of independence would remove that support and raise the cost of the debt stock.
claims.indicator: central bank independence, sovereign debt-to-GDP and yields
claims.direction: weaker independence leads to higher yields at given debt
claims.testable: partly - cross-country independence indices versus debt tolerance

claims.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
claims.quote: Venod Kosla the venture capitalist he believes that computer will be free labor will be free on the back of robots and so on
claims.claim: Some technologists (Vinod Khosla, per the host) argue that AI and robots will make computing and labor effectively free, an extreme deflationary view that the host raises against Rogoff's expectation of lasting inflation.
claims.indicator: AI and robotics effect on labor costs
